q: How do you perform a rolling upgrade of OpenStack with minimal downtime?
a: I treat an upgrade as a project with rehearsal. First I read the release notes for removed options and database migrations, back up the databases and configuration, and run the whole upgrade in staging. In production, I upgrade in a defined order. Control-plane services go first, with expand schema migrations run online, services restarted one controller at a time behind HAProxy, using oslo.versionedobjects so new and old versions can coexist. Then the compute nodes are upgraded in batches after draining or accepting a brief agent restart, since running guests are not affected by restarting nova-compute. Finally I run the contract migrations and cleanup, and remove deprecated config. Throughout, I run smoke tests and canaries, watch error rates, keep rollback to previous images or packages ready, and avoid mixing releases longer than necessary. SLURP lets me skip intermediate releases.
f: Why can old and new services coexist?
What is the expand and contract migration pattern?
p: Rehearse in staging, back up, upgrade the control plane one node at a time, then computes in batches, run contract migrations, and canary throughout. Versioned objects allow temporary mixed versions.
tip: Mention upgrade checks and online data migrations by name.

q: How do you monitor OpenStack: which metrics and alerts matter most?
a: I monitor in layers. At the infrastructure layer, host CPU, memory, disk, network and hardware health through node exporter and IPMI. At the platform layer, service state: nova-compute, neutron agents and cinder-volume heartbeat, API response codes and latency per endpoint, RabbitMQ queue depth and consumers, Galera cluster size and flow control, HAProxy backends, and Ceph health, slow ops and capacity. At the capacity layer, hypervisor vCPU and RAM allocation versus overcommit, Placement usage, floating IP and fixed IP pool consumption, and quotas near limits. At the tenant experience layer, a synthetic canary that boots a VM and pings it, with success rate and duration, which I consider the single most valuable alert. I use Prometheus with the OpenStack exporter and Grafana, alert on symptoms first, and write a runbook link into every alert.
f: Why is the canary so valuable?
Which alert would page the on-call?
p: Layered monitoring: hosts, service heartbeats and API latency, RabbitMQ, Galera and Ceph health, capacity versus allocation, and a synthetic boot-and-ping canary that mirrors the tenant experience.
tip: The synthetic canary is the alert that reflects users.

q: What are Ceilometer, Gnocchi and Aodh, and how do they relate to billing and autoscaling?
a: Ceilometer collects telemetry, meaning samples and events from OpenStack services and instances, such as CPU time, network bytes and disk use. Gnocchi is a time-series database designed to store those measures efficiently, aggregated by resource and archive policy. Aodh evaluates alarm rules on the metrics or events and triggers actions like webhooks or Heat scaling policies. CloudKitty then rates the usage into billing or showback data. Together they power tenant autoscaling, usage reports and chargeback. However, in many modern clouds the operational monitoring has moved to Prometheus, and Ceilometer plus Gnocchi is used where billing or Heat autoscaling is needed, because Gnocchi had scaling and maintenance challenges in large deployments. When asked, I explain what each does and note that you can choose a lighter path depending on the requirement.
f: Why do many operators prefer Prometheus now?
What does CloudKitty do?
p: Ceilometer collects, Gnocchi stores time series, Aodh alarms and triggers, CloudKitty rates usage. They support billing and Heat autoscaling; Prometheus often replaces them for operational monitoring.
cmds: openstack alarm create --name cpu-high --type gnocchi_resources_threshold --metric cpu --threshold 70000000000 --resource-type instance --resource-id <id>
tip: Separate operational monitoring from usage metering.

q: How do you handle capacity planning and chargeback or showback?
a: Capacity planning compares supply to demand with forecasts. I track allocation, meaning what is promised through flavors and quotas, and utilisation, meaning what is actually used, for vCPU, RAM, disk and network, per aggregate and per availability zone. I use trends and growth projects from onboarding pipelines to estimate when I will cross thresholds, typically setting a trigger at 70 to 80 percent allocation, and I factor in lead time for hardware procurement, which can be months. I also keep failure headroom. For chargeback or showback, I use CloudKitty or exported usage to attribute cost per project, with unit prices by flavor, volume type and floating IP. Showing teams their cost changes behaviour even without invoices, by encouraging shutdown of idle instances. Regular reviews with tenants tune quotas and sizes to real needs.
f: Why track both allocation and utilisation?
What lead time should drive thresholds?
p: Track allocation and utilisation per aggregate, forecast growth against procurement lead time, keep failure headroom, and use CloudKitty or exports for showback to change tenant behaviour.
tip: Say hardware lead time sets your capacity thresholds.

q: How do you patch the OS and kernel on hosts in a running cloud?
a: I plan patching as a rolling operation across failure domains. For compute nodes, I drain one host at a time or one rack at a time, live-migrating instances away, then patch, reboot, verify services, and return it to service, using automation that checks health before moving on. For controllers, I patch one at a time, confirming that the cluster is healthy, Galera synced, RabbitMQ rejoined, and the VIP stable, before the next. Storage nodes are done carefully, one failure domain at a time, setting noout in Ceph so a reboot does not trigger data movement, and waiting for the cluster to return to health. Kernel and hypervisor updates for security fixes get higher priority, and I track the CVE exposure. I keep a patch calendar, test on staging first, and report compliance, because unpatched hosts become a compliance and security problem.
f: Why set noout before rebooting an OSD host?
What do you check between controller reboots?
p: Patch one failure domain at a time with health gates: drain and migrate computes, patch controllers sequentially with Galera, RabbitMQ and VIP checks, and use Ceph noout for storage reboots.
tip: Mention health gates between each node.

q: How do you tune the performance of a busy OpenStack cloud?
a: I measure first, then tune the biggest bottleneck. On the control plane, I look at API latency per service, database slow queries and connection counts, RabbitMQ queue depth, and worker utilisation. Typical fixes are more API and conductor workers sized to CPU, tuned DB connection pools, indexes or archiving old rows, which is the purpose of nova-manage db archive_deleted_rows and purge, moving to OVN to cut agent chatter, and caching with memcached. On compute, I tune CPU governors, NUMA and pinning for sensitive workloads, hugepages, virtio multiqueue, and disk cache modes. In networking, I enable jumbo frames, offloads, and tune conntrack tables. In storage, I look at Ceph latency, OSD CPU, network speed, and use separate pools for different tiers. Every change is made one at a time, measured with Rally or application tests, and recorded.
f: Why archive deleted rows?
What does virtio multiqueue improve?
p: Measure, find the bottleneck, then tune workers, DB pools and archiving, memcached, OVN, NUMA and hugepages, jumbo frames and Ceph tiers, one change at a time with before and after tests.
tip: One change at a time, measured, is the discipline to highlight.

q: How do you onboard a new tenant or team into the cloud consistently?
a: I make it a self-service or automated workflow, so every tenant starts with the same secure baseline. A request, from a ticket or a portal, triggers automation that creates the project in the right domain, creates groups mapped to the identity provider, assigns roles, sets quotas by size, creates a default network with a router and subnet, a default security group with sensible rules, and keys and tags for ownership and cost centre. Notifications go to the team with documentation and endpoints. Naming standards and tags make reporting possible. I also set policy for who can create public networks and floating IPs, and for image sources. The automation is code in Git, idempotent, and every step is logged for audit. Later, offboarding follows the reverse process, snapshotting if needed and freeing resources, so abandoned projects do not consume capacity.
f: Why map groups from the IdP?
How do you handle offboarding?
p: Automate project creation, role assignment via IdP groups, quotas, default network and security group, and tags for owner and cost centre, with logging and a matching offboarding flow.
tip: Mention offboarding to show lifecycle thinking.

q: How do you manage logs centrally and use them to troubleshoot OpenStack?
a: I ship logs from every node and container to a central store such as Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, or Loki, using an agent like Fluentd, Filebeat or Promtail. Parsing extracts fields like service, level, request ID, instance UUID and project, so I can search across components. During an incident I start with the request ID from a failing API call and follow it through Nova, Neutron, Cinder and Glance in one query, which turns a multi-service puzzle into a timeline. I set retention by value, longer for audit and security logs, shorter for debug, and I keep debug off by default because it floods storage and may log sensitive data. Dashboards show error rates per service, and alerts trigger on patterns such as repeated MessagingTimeout or 'No valid host'. Time synchronisation across nodes is essential for readable timelines.
f: Why must clocks be synchronised?
What should alerts match in logs?
p: Central log store with parsed request ID, instance and project fields; follow a request ID across services; alert on MessagingTimeout and No valid host patterns; keep debug off by default.
cmds: kubectl logs -n openstack deploy/nova-api | grep req-
journalctl -u docker --since '10 min ago' | grep ERROR
tip: Request ID correlation is the standout technique.

q: How do you clean up orphaned resources and stale data in OpenStack?
a: Clouds accumulate orphans: volumes and ports of deleted instances, floating IPs not associated, stale images, deleted rows in the database and abandoned projects. I tackle it with scheduled reports and safe automation. Reports list unattached volumes older than a threshold, down ports, unused floating IPs, instances in ERROR for days, and projects with no activity. Owners are notified first, with a grace period, and resources are tagged. Cleanup of database soft-deleted rows uses archive and purge commands to keep tables small. For leaked or inconsistent resources between services, I use the documented tools, such as the Neutron or Nova database consistency checks, rather than manual SQL. Every cleanup is logged and reversible where possible, for example by snapshotting volumes before deleting. The goal is cost control, performance and security hygiene without surprising tenants.
f: How do you avoid deleting something still in use?
What does purge do?
p: Scheduled reports of unattached volumes, idle IPs, error instances and dormant projects, notify owners with a grace period, archive and purge DB rows, and use official consistency tools.
tip: Notify owners and keep it reversible.

q: How do you manage image lifecycles and golden images?
a: I build images through a pipeline instead of by hand: Packer or diskimage-builder takes a base distribution, applies configuration, installs cloud-init, agents and hardening, runs tests, and uploads the result to Glance with properties and tags. Images are rebuilt on a schedule, for example monthly, and when critical vulnerabilities appear, and each build is versioned by date and recorded in a manifest. Old images are deprecated through visibility settings and tags, and eventually removed after tenants have moved. I mark which images are supported, and set required properties such as hw_disk_bus or os_distro for correct virtual hardware. Signing images and validating signatures in Nova stops tampered images from booting. Documentation tells tenants how to find the latest image, and an alert flags instances running an image that is out of support.
f: How do you deprecate an image safely?
What does image signature verification protect against?
p: Build with Packer or diskimage-builder in a tested pipeline, version and rebuild monthly and on CVEs, deprecate via visibility, sign and verify, and flag instances running old images.
cmds: openstack image set --property os_distro=ubuntu --tag supported ubuntu-2026-10
tip: Pipelines, signing and deprecation are the three points.

q: How do you restore service after losing the whole database?
a: I stay calm and follow a tested runbook. First, stop the OpenStack services that write to the database, so nothing further changes while I restore. Then I restore the most recent consistent backup, for a Galera cluster that usually means restoring on one node, bootstrapping the cluster from it, and letting the other nodes rejoin through state transfer. If I also have binary logs, I can replay to a point in time and reduce data loss. After the database is back, I start services and then reconcile reality with records: instances that were created after the backup may exist on hypervisors but not in the database, and instances deleted later may reappear. I compare libvirt domains, Ceph images and ports with the restored records, clean up or re-adopt orphans, and tell tenants about any lost changes. The lesson is frequent backups, tested restores and a documented RPO.
f: How do you handle drift between hypervisors and the restored DB?
What is point-in-time recovery?
p: Stop writers, restore the last consistent backup, bootstrap Galera from it, apply binlogs if available, then reconcile hypervisor, Ceph and port reality against the restored records.
tip: Reconciliation after restore is the step people forget.

q: What does a good change-management and maintenance-window process look like for a cloud?
a: Every change to the platform goes through a lightweight but real process. A change request describes what, why, the risk, the rollback and the test plan, and is peer reviewed. Changes are implemented from code in Git through the deployment tool, first in staging and then production, in a published maintenance window with notice to tenants, scaled to impact. During the window I follow a checklist with validation steps, keep a live log, and have a clear abort point at which I roll back. Afterwards, a short review records the outcome and updates runbooks. For emergency changes there is an expedited path, with retrospective review. Good communication matters as much as the technical steps: a status page, advance notices and clear closure messages build the trust that makes maintenance easier to schedule next time.
f: What defines the abort point?
How do emergency changes differ?
p: Reviewed change requests with risk, test and rollback, applied from Git via the deployment tool, staged first, with tenant notice, a checklist and an abort point, then a short review.
tip: Communication is as important as the technical steps.

q: How do you keep OpenStack documentation and runbooks useful and current?
a: Runbooks decay quickly unless they are part of the workflow. I keep them in Git next to the automation, written as short, step-by-step procedures with prerequisites, commands, expected output, and rollback, and I link them from alerts so the on-call engineer lands on the right page. Where possible, I turn a runbook into code, such as an Ansible playbook, so the doc describes the script instead of replacing it. Every incident ends with a review that includes updating or creating a runbook. I schedule quarterly walk-throughs where someone who did not write the runbook follows it in staging, and fix every unclear step. Architecture diagrams, IP plans and decision records are versioned alongside. The measure of success is that a new on-call engineer can resolve a common failure using the document alone.
f: How do you test a runbook?
What belongs in an architecture decision record?
p: Runbooks live in Git, are linked from alerts, are turned into playbooks where possible, updated after every incident, and tested by someone who did not write them.
tip: Tested-by-a-newcomer is the best quality signal.

q: How do you harden an OpenStack deployment?
a: I work through layers. Identity: enforce secure RBAC, MFA through federation, application credentials for automation, and short token lifetimes. Network: isolate management, storage and tenant networks, restrict the API endpoints with firewalls, TLS for all endpoints including internal, and no direct database or queue exposure. Hosts: minimal OS, regular patches, SELinux or AppArmor enforcing, hardened SSH with keys only, CIS benchmarks, and disabled unused services. Services: run as non-root, containers with limited capabilities, secrets in a vault and encrypted at rest, and sensible default security groups. Data: volume encryption with Barbican, backups encrypted. Operations: central audit logging, intrusion detection, quotas, rate limits, and a vulnerability management process following OpenStack security advisories. I validate with periodic reviews against the OpenStack Security Guide.
f: Which standard would you benchmark against?
How do you monitor security advisories?
p: Secure RBAC and MFA, network isolation and TLS everywhere, hardened hosts with SELinux, secrets in a vault, encrypted volumes, audit logs and a patching process aligned with the Security Guide.
tip: Offer a layered list, then name the Security Guide.

q: What is Barbican and how does it manage secrets and keys?
a: Barbican is the OpenStack key manager. It stores and manages secrets such as passwords, certificates, symmetric keys and private keys, with access control through Keystone. A secret has a payload, metadata and an optional expiry, and is stored encrypted through a plugin back end: the simple crypto plugin using a master key, a PKCS#11 hardware security module, or Vault integration. Other services use it: Cinder and Nova for encrypted volumes, Octavia for TLS listener certificates, Glance for image signing and Magnum for cluster certificates. Containers group related secrets, for example a certificate with its key. Access is controlled by project and role, and ACLs can share a secret with specific users. Because it holds the keys to many other protections, Barbican itself needs to be highly available, backed up, and protected with an HSM for sensitive environments.
f: Which services depend on Barbican?
Why consider an HSM back end?
p: Barbican stores secrets and keys with Keystone access control and pluggable encrypted back ends. It supports encrypted volumes, Octavia TLS, image signing and Magnum certificates.
cmds: openstack secret container create --type certificate --secret certificate=<ref> --secret private_key=<ref> --name cert1
tip: Say it holds keys for many services, so it must be HA and backed up.

q: How do you isolate tenants from each other in OpenStack?
a: Isolation exists at several layers. Compute: each instance runs in its own KVM guest with hardware virtualisation, with SELinux sVirt or AppArmor confining the QEMU process, so a guest escape is contained. Network: tenant networks are separate segments, VXLAN, Geneve or VLAN, with security groups and port security preventing spoofing, and private routers so overlapping address ranges are isolated. Storage: volumes are owned by projects and access is by project scope, with optional encryption per volume. Identity: Keystone projects and domains with RBAC. For stronger isolation, I use dedicated host aggregates so sensitive tenants do not share hypervisors, disable memory deduplication features, and sometimes use bare metal through Ironic. Quotas and QoS reduce noisy-neighbour effects. Isolation is a combination of defaults and careful configuration, not a single switch.
f: What does sVirt do?
When would you dedicate hosts to a tenant?
p: KVM guests confined by sVirt or AppArmor, separate network segments with security groups and port security, project-scoped storage and RBAC, and dedicated aggregates or bare metal for the most sensitive tenants.
tip: Say isolation is layered: compute, network, storage, identity.

q: How do you audit activity in OpenStack?
a: Auditing needs a record of who did what, when and from where. I enable the audit middleware, based on pycadf, which emits CADF-format events for API calls to the message bus or log, including user, project, action and outcome. I send those logs, plus Keystone authentication events, system auth logs and host audit logs from auditd, to a central write-once store or SIEM, with retention set by policy. Alerts cover privilege changes, role assignments, failed logins, creation of application credentials, and API calls from unusual locations. Time synchronisation keeps timelines accurate, and request IDs tie operations together. I also make sure administrators use named accounts, never a shared admin, so accountability is possible. Periodic access reviews check who holds elevated roles. Protecting the audit logs from tampering is part of the design.
f: What is CADF?
Why avoid a shared admin account?
p: Enable audit middleware for CADF events, centralise API, Keystone, auditd and auth logs in a tamper-resistant store, alert on role changes and failed logins, and use named admin accounts.
tip: Named accounts and tamper-resistant storage are the key points.

q: How do you respond to an OpenStack security advisory (OSSA) or a critical CVE?
a: I follow a defined process. First, triage: read the advisory, identify the affected services and versions, and check whether my deployment is exposed, which depends on configuration and network reachability. Second, assess severity and exploitability, for example whether it requires authentication, and decide a timeline. Third, find the fix: a backported patch in my release branch, an updated container image or distribution package, or a configuration mitigation if the patch is not ready. Fourth, test in staging, then roll out through the normal deployment tool, in batches, with monitoring. Fifth, verify that the vulnerable version is gone and record the change. For critical issues, I accelerate through an emergency change path and consider temporary controls like firewall rules. Subscribing to the OpenStack security announcements list and my vendor's feed keeps me informed.
f: How do you mitigate before a patch exists?
How do you verify the fix is deployed everywhere?
p: Triage exposure, assess severity, get the backported fix or a mitigation, test in staging, roll out in batches, verify the fixed version everywhere, and document. Use an emergency path for critical issues.
tip: Say exposure assessment comes before panic patching.

q: How do you secure the hypervisor and the compute host?
a: The compute host is a high-value target because it holds many tenants. I install a minimal OS, keep it patched, and allow only required ports, with management access through a bastion or jump host. SELinux in enforcing mode with sVirt gives each QEMU process a unique label, so one guest cannot access another's files. I disable unnecessary services, restrict who can use libvirt, and protect the libvirt and migration channels with TLS or SSH. Kernel hardening and mitigations for CPU side-channel vulnerabilities are applied, with awareness of performance effects, and for the highest isolation, I disable simultaneous multithreading or schedule tenants on separate hosts. Secure boot, a TPM and measured boot help detect tampering. The BMC network is isolated since BMC compromise bypasses the OS. Regular compliance scans confirm the configuration remains hardened.
f: Why isolate the BMC network?
What are CPU side-channel mitigations?
p: Minimal patched OS, SELinux sVirt, libvirt access controls and TLS, kernel and side-channel mitigations, secure boot, isolated BMC network and regular compliance scans.
tip: Mention the BMC network; it is often overlooked.

q: How do you protect the OpenStack APIs from abuse and denial of service?
a: I combine edge and internal controls. At the edge, a load balancer or WAF applies rate limits per client IP, connection and request size limits, and blocks malformed requests, with public API endpoints reachable only where needed, sometimes only from corporate networks or a VPN. Inside, Keystone and service middleware can throttle, and quotas limit what one tenant can create. I monitor for spikes in authentication failures and API errors, and set alerts for unusual request rates by project. I separate public and internal endpoints, so internal service traffic is not affected by public load. Worker and queue limits prevent one expensive call type from starving others, and long operations are asynchronous. For incidents, I can quickly block an abusive source at the firewall and disable a compromised application credential. Testing with load tools shows where the limits actually are.
f: How do quotas help with API abuse?
How do you block a compromised credential quickly?
p: Rate limit and cap connections at HAProxy or a WAF, restrict public exposure, use quotas and middleware throttling, separate internal and public endpoints, and alert on auth failure spikes.
tip: Separate public and internal endpoints to contain load.

q: How do you handle secrets inside instances and automation without leaking them?
a: Never bake secrets into images or user data in plain text, since user data is readable from the metadata service by anything in the guest and by project members through the API. Instead I deliver secrets at runtime from a secret manager, such as Barbican or Vault, and let the instance prove its identity, for example through a short-lived token or an approle bound to the instance metadata. For automation, I use application credentials with narrow roles and an expiry, stored in the CI secret store, never in the repository, and clouds.yaml files with restricted permissions. I rotate credentials regularly and after staff changes, and scan repositories for leaked secrets. Logs must not print secrets, so debug logging is disabled in production. Finally, I assume leaks will happen and design for fast revocation and small blast radius.
f: Why is user data not a safe place for secrets?
How can an instance authenticate to Vault?
p: Deliver secrets at runtime from Barbican or Vault with short-lived identity, avoid secrets in images or user data, use scoped expiring application credentials, rotate, scan repos and plan for revocation.
tip: Remember user data is readable; do not put secrets there.
